newsitem.title: UK: UK shares face uphill battle after tight budget.
newsitem.headline: UK shares face uphill battle after tight budget.

text.p: The UK equity market got largely what it expected from Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's budget on Tuesday but strategists warned shares remain prey to Wall Street jitters and worries over the direction of interest rates.

Much of Clarke's fiscally tight package had already been anticipated and strategists said further gains for the benchmark FTSE 100 stock index may be hard to come by,after it hit a record high of 4,094.4 in early trading today.
"Clarke is being the good guy again," said Bob Semple, strategist at NatWest Securities.
"It's a responsible budget. The trouble is that the market went up in anticipation of it. I think we're at the top of the range and a lot will depend on the international environment."
Clarke's budget forecast a drop in government borrowing next year, continued low inflation and accelerating economic growth, with his forecasts mostly in line with market expectations.
He said it had been an "eye-wateringly tight public spending round" and said a "fiscal stimulus at this stage could be just as damaging as letting go of monetary policy."
But budget measures had a sharp impact on individual stocks and sectors.
Among those hit were electrical retailer Dixons, which fell 23-1/2p to 547 after Clarke promised measures to make sure VAT is paid on extended warranties.

And a decision not to cut beer duties, as well as a 40 percent tax rise on "alcopops" weighed on brewing-to-hotels group Bass, down 11p 803-1/2. Alcoholic soft drinks have proved one of Bass's fastest-growth areas.
The past three days have seen UK stocks surge amid hopes that a tough budget would help calm fears that interest rates will rise sharply next year to slow growth and head off inflationary pressures.

Strategists pointed out the budget came at a critical time for UK markets, ahead of an election which must be held by May next year and amid concerns that strong growth may push up inflation during 1997.
"It is an important budget for the markets because it is the last before the election," said Steve Wright, strategist at brokerage BZW.
Yet by the close of trading in London, the market's attention had already been diverted to New York, where the Dow fell as much as 50 points in a retreat from recent record-breaking gains.

The FTSE ended up 13.8 points at 4,068.4, having been up 32.0 points as Clarke began delivering his budget at 1532 GMT. The December futures contract on the FTSE, which closes after the cash market, ended up 34.0 from up 42.0 as the speech began.

"There were no surprises at all," said Scott Evans, strategist with UBS. "The budget has already been discounted by the market. It's fairly valued here, but probably will take its lead from the gilt market." Some other traders and strategists cast doubt on the budget's long-term significance. "The key driving force in the short-term will be the U.S. market," said one trader. "That will have more of an impact on the UK market than this budget."

Richard Davidson, strategist at Morgan Stanley said: "There is no country in the world that places so much emphasis on the budget as this one does, there are some valid historic reasons but the ballyhoo that surrounds it is perplexing and the amount of time devoted to analysing it is just incredible."
"It may cause some short-term fluctuations (in the markets) but generally budgets don't make any difference to the long-term investment case."
